en: The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
and Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Dharma-bhadra, in accordance with the Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now, for your sake, proclaim the profound, definitive, and true meaning (which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its significance is deep and far-reaching; it is pure, unadulterated, complete, and possesses the characteristics of the stainless Brahma-faring). Listen attentively and reflect upon it well!"
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
What is called the definitive, correct meaning?"
"We wish to hear this; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The meaning of 'definitive' (niyata) is as follows:"

The five aggregates, the five aggregates of clinging, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four noble truths, the twenty-two faculties, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four dhyāna concentrations, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurable practices, the four unhindered knowledges, the four meditative absorptions, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Such dharmas as these are called the definitive correct meaning.
"The five aggregates" refers to:
the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
These are called the five aggregates. The five aggregates of clinging are:

the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
These are called the five aggregates of clinging.
"The eighteen elements" refer to:
the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element;
The ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element;
the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element.
The body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
These are called the eighteen elements.
"The twelve bases (āyatana) are as follows:
the internal base of the eye and the external base of forms;
the internal base of the ear and the external base of sounds;..."
The internal nose base and the external odor base;
the internal tongue base and the external flavor base;
the internal body base and the external tangible base.
The internal sense base of mind and the external sense base of phenomena—
these are called the twelve bases.
"Dependent origination in twelve links" refers to:
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise.
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases;
the six sense bases condition contact;
contact conditions feeling.
Feeling conditions craving;
craving conditions clinging;
clinging conditions becoming.
With birth as condition, there is aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair; thus this entire great mass of suffering arises.
By reason of these conditions, the phenomena of the aggregates exist; if these conditions were absent, the phenomena of the aggregates would cease.
That is to say:
with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of grasping comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress. Thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"These various phenomena arise and cease with ignorance as their condition.
What serves as the condition?
It is the lack of understanding regarding the past limit, the lack of understanding regarding the future limit, and the lack of understanding regarding the middle limit."
They do not understand internal phenomena, they do not understand external phenomena, and they do not understand both internal and external phenomena;
they do not understand wholesome karma, they do not understand unwholesome karma, and they do not understand both wholesome and unwholesome karma;
they do not understand causes, they do not understand effects, and they do not understand both causes and effects.

They do not comprehend conditioned phenomena that have already arisen, they do not comprehend conditioned phenomena that have not yet arisen, and they do not comprehend conditioned phenomena currently arising;
they do not comprehend the Buddha, they do not comprehend the Dharma, and they do not comprehend the Saṅgha;

they do not comprehend the phenomenon of suffering, they do not comprehend the phenomenon of its origin, they do not comprehend the phenomenon of its cessation, and they do not comprehend the phenomenon of the path.
They do not comprehend wholesome dharmas; they do not comprehend unwholesome dharmas;
they do not comprehend dharmas that entail fault; they do not comprehend dharmas that entail merit;
they do not comprehend dharmas that should be practiced; they do not comprehend dharmas that should not be practiced.
They do not understand phenomena of high and low;
they do not understand conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
Not understanding in this way, they are unable to give rise to signless wisdom regarding phenomena such as black and white.
"Because of this ignorance, one is unable to awaken to reality; it constitutes a fault that even obstructs suchness-knowledge (yathābhūta-jñāna), preventing the realization of the quiescent nirvāṇa."

This ignorance has a nature of delusive darkness and is a purely singular state of folly; it is like a blind person walking only upon a dark path, accumulating various defilements that diminish wisdom and rendering one unable to transcend all obstructing phenomena.

Moreover, this ignorance acts as an obstruction to clarity; ignorance is suffering and pain, ignorance is a vessel of poison, ignorance is a binding cord, ignorance is the root of poison, ignorance is a poisonous tree, ignorance is the fundamental affliction (*mūlakleśa*), ignorance is the basis of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), ignorance is the locus of inversion, ignorance is a dark chamber, and ignorance is the gloom of delusion (*moha*).
Such meanings as these are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
With this as a condition, the phenomena of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.
As for these volitional formations, there are three types.
That is to say:
bodily formations, vocal formations, and mental formations.
As for bodily formations:
Inhalation and exhalation depend upon the body and are bound to the body; because they depend upon the body, inhalation and exhalation are termed "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
As for "vocal formations" (*vāksaṃskāra*), this refers to debate and discrimination; that is, the words used for such debate and discrimination are therefore called vocal formations.
Mental formations (*manasikāra*) refer to mental factors such as greed, hatred, and delusion, which rely upon the mind and are bound to the mind.
Because they rely upon the mind, they are designated as "mental formations."
"Furthermore, there are three practices.
What are the three? They are as follows:"
Wholesome formations, unwholesome formations, and imperturbable formations—
these are called the three formations.
"With formations as condition, the dharma of consciousness arises."
Regarding the dharmas of consciousness, there are six kinds of consciousness, namely:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; these are called the six consciousnesses.
"With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
'Name-and-form' refers to the aggregate of form,
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness."
"Form" refers to the five internal sense objects, all of which are composed of the four great elements.
The four great elements refer to:
Earth, water, fire, and wind. The essence of earth is solidity and heaviness;
the nature of water is flowing and moisture; warmth constitutes fire; and movement is called wind.
The five sense objects (pañca-viṣaya) formed by these four great elements are termed the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
Furthermore, among these aggregates, four aggregates are called "name" (nāma) and one aggregate is called "form" (rūpa); thus, these five aggregates are termed "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
"With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise."
The six sense bases refer to the six internal sense bases:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
These are called the six sense bases.
“With the six sense bases as condition, the phenomenon of contact arises.
There are six kinds of contact, namely:
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.”
These are called contact (*sparśa*).
With contact as a condition, the phenomena of feeling (*vedanā*) arise.
There are three kinds of feeling, namely:
Painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neutral feeling.
Thus, conditioned by eye-contact, these three feelings arise; and so it is for all [sense bases] up to and including mind-contact.
This is called feeling.
"With feeling as condition, craving arises.
There are six kinds of craving,
namely:"
The eye perceives forms, the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue discerns tastes, the body feels tangibles, and the mind discriminates phenomena.
Through craving for these six things, it is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
"With craving as condition, the phenomena of clinging arise.
There are four kinds of clinging, namely:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to the doctrine of self."
Because craving increases, it is called "clinging.
With clinging as a condition, the dharma of "existence" arises.
There are three types of existence:
There are existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"Existence in the desire realm" refers to the ten evil destinies, as well as humans and devas.
"The ten evil destinies refer to the eight hells:
first, Saṃjīva (Reviving);
second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope)."
3. Saṃghāta (Crushing);
4. Raurava (Wailing);
5. Mahāraurava (Great Wailing).
Sixth, the Reviving Hell;
seventh, the Great Reviving Hell;
eighth, the Uninterrupted Hell.
9. The realm of animals;
10. The realm of hungry ghosts.
These ten kinds are called the evil destinies.
"The human realm consists of the four great continents:
Jambudvīpa in the south, Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north."
Jambudvīpa measures seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the configuration of this continent is broad in the north and narrow in the south, resembling the shape of a chariot.
Pūrvavideha measures eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the configuration of that continent resembles a half-moon.
The continent of Aparagoyānī is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its shape is like that of the full moon.
The continent of Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its shape is square and straight, like a pond.
These four continents are called the human realm.
As for the celestial realm: it consists of the six heavens of the desire realm.
That is to say:

the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; these are called the six heavens of the desire realm.
These various realms of existence are called the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are eighteen heavens, namely:

The Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, the Heaven of the Brahma-assistants, the Great Brahma Heaven, the Heaven of Light, the Heaven of Infinite Light, the Heaven of Pervasive Light, the Heaven of Purity, the Heaven of Infinite Purity, the Heaven of Universal Purity, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven of Vast Fruit, the Heaven of Non-conception, the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven Without Heat, the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation, the Heaven of Excellent Vision, and the Heaven of the Ultimate of Form.
These various devas are called the realm of form-existence (*rūpabhava*).
As for the realm of formless-existence (*ārūpyabhava*), there are four kinds of devas, namely:
The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception—
these various gods are called the formless existence (*ārūpya-bhava*).
These three realms of existence are thus designated as "existence.
With existence as a condition, the dharma of birth arises.

"Birth" refers to the fact that when sentient beings discard these aggregates, they reappear with the characteristics of aggregates within a realm or destiny according to the retribution of their karma; therefore, it is called "birth."
"With birth as a condition, aging and death come to be.

As for 'aging,' it refers to the maturation of the fruits of the aggregates of sentient beings; their consciousness becomes deluded and confused, they forget much, their hair turns white and their faces wrinkle, their physical strength becomes feeble, they must lean on a staff when moving about, they gasp and moan, their vitality gradually diminishes, and their faculties decay—this is called aging."
Furthermore, what is called death?

It refers to when sentient beings, according to the karma they have summoned, reach the exhaustion of their lifespan; consciousness abandons its appropriation, the life-faculty perishes, and the aggregates disperse—this is called death.
That is to say:
old age has no fixed characteristic of its own; it is established as a link in dependence upon death. Because these two phenomena merge into one, they are called "old age and death.
This is what is termed the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
"Furthermore, what are called the four noble truths? They are:
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin [of suffering], the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path."
The Truth of Suffering consists of:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Sufferings such as these are called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As for the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), it refers to the phenomenon of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Because of this craving, one gives rise to attachment; because of this attachment, one initiates karma and moistens rebirth, gathering [the causes] together as their source—this is called the Truth of Origination.
The Truth of Cessation refers to the complete eradication of the phenomena of craving and all other afflictions, thereby realizing the principle of quiescence; this is called the Truth of Cessation.
The Truth of the Path consists of the Eightfold Noble Path.
That is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
These Eightfold Noble Path factors are called the Truth of the Path.
These Four Truths, which can be contemplated through noble wisdom, are called the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, what are the twenty-two faculties? They are as follows:

The eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, male faculty, female faculty, life faculty, mind faculty, faculty of pleasant feeling, faculty of painful feeling, faculty of joyous feeling, faculty of sorrowful feeling, faculty of equanimity, faculty of faith, faculty of energy, faculty of mindfulness, faculty of concentration, faculty of wisdom, faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," faculty of "knowing," and faculty of "one who has known."
These are called the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśatīndriya*).
Furthermore, what are the ten powers (*daśabala*)?
They refer to the Tathāgata’s wisdom that, regarding the dharmas of what is possible and what is impossible for sentient beings, understands them as they truly are.
This is called the Tathāgata’s first power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

Furthermore, regarding all the karmic actions of sentient beings throughout the past, present, and future, as well as the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions for their births in various places, the Buddha understands them all completely through his power of knowledge.
This is called the Tathāgata’s second power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma.

Furthermore, regarding all dharmas of meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti, as well as the dharmas that exhaust all outflows, the Buddha, by means of his power of knowledge, understands them as they truly are.
This is called the Tathāgata’s third power of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, regarding the various distinctions among the faculties and natures of all classes of sentient beings—whether superior or inferior—the Buddha, by means of his power of wisdom, knows them as they truly are.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fourth power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the various and diverse inclinations and understandings possessed by all classes of sentient beings, the Buddha knows them as they truly are through his power of knowledge.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power of knowledge regarding the strength of faith and understanding.

Furthermore, regarding all the various distinctions among the realms and destinies of sentient beings, the Buddha, by means of his power of knowledge, understands them as they truly are; this is called the Tathāgata’s sixth power of knowledge regarding the realms and destinies.
"Furthermore, regarding all the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, by means of his power of wisdom, knows them as they truly are.
This is called the Tathāgata’s seventh power of knowledge regarding inclinations and desires."
"Furthermore, throughout immeasurable and incalculable past eons, the Tathāgata has known all the various matters concerning sentient beings—namely:
one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, and hundreds of thousands of births, up to incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of births."

In this manner, throughout countless eons of formation and eons of destruction, sentient beings die here and are born there, or die there and are born here; even their clans, noble or low status, names, food and drink, pleasure and pain, and the length of their lifespans—all possess such characteristics and such causes and conditions.
In this way, regarding the various events throughout immeasurable past ages, the Buddha is able to know them all completely through his power of wisdom.
This is called the Tathāgata’s eighth power of knowledge: the knowledge of past lives.

"Furthermore, with his purified divine eye, the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings—whether noble or base, high or low, beautiful or ugly, arising or ceasing—and whether they are born into the good realms or fall into the evil destinies."
Furthermore, those sentient beings perform various karmic actions, namely:
unwholesome physical karma, committing various perverse deeds;
and unwholesome verbal karma, slandering the noble and holy ones.
Unwholesome mental karma arises from wrong views.
Due to these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one falls into the evil realms.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds with their bodies and do not engage in wrongful conduct;
One performs wholesome karma with the mouth by not slandering the noble ones;
one performs wholesome karma with the mind by giving rise to right view.
By these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one is reborn in the realms of humans or devas.
Such matters as these, the Tathāgata is able to perceive entirely with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
This is called the Tathāgata’s ninth power of knowledge, the power of the divine eye.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows that those sentient beings have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), having realized untainted liberation and liberation through wisdom. By means of his own supernormal power, he realizes this Dharma: "Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence."
Such phenomena as these, the Buddha is able to fully comprehend through his power of wisdom.
This is called the Tathāgata’s tenth power of knowledge:

the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*). By means of these ten powers, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, what are called the four fearlessnesses?
They are as follows: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaims these words:

"By means of my own wisdom, having traversed the path of reality, I have attained perfect enlightenment and let out the lion's roar, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma; there is no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, human, māra, or Brahmā who is able to equal me."
This is called the Tathāgata’s fearlessness regarding all-knowledge.

The Tathāgata has already attained the fruit of the Dharma—the merit of the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace and tranquility; his outflows are exhausted, and both seeds and habitual tendencies have perished. This is called the Tathāgata’s fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows.
“Furthermore, the Tathāgata reveals the path to suffering for the assembly of śrāvakas, teaching the exhaustion of afflictions and the ultimate limit of suffering.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering.”
“Furthermore, the Tathāgata teaches all obstructive dharmas to the śrāvakas, enabling them to emerge from them.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path.
These are known as the four fearlessnesses.”
Furthermore, what are called the four dhyānas? They are:
being detached from all desires and all defiled phenomena, and eliminating doubt, conceptualization, and discursive thought.
This is called the first meditative absorption of joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Furthermore, having abandoned desire and eliminated discursive thoughts, one should cause all external phenomena to completely vanish and the internal mind to be tranquil; by integrating both internal and external phenomena, they are all brought back into a single unity.
This is called the second dhyāna, the concentration of joy and bliss born of meditative absorption.
Furthermore, one relinquishes the perception of joy and bliss, and experiences bliss throughout the body without any mental grasping.
This is called the third meditative absorption, which is the sublime happiness detached from joy.
Furthermore, by abandoning both suffering and pleasure, and being free from the perceptions of sorrow and joy, all phenomena become pure.
This is called the fourth meditative absorption, the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
These are called the four dhyāna concentrations.
Furthermore, what are called the four formless concentrations? They are as follows:

Cultivating that concentration, one becomes weary of the lower forms and takes delight in the higher formless states; because these are formless, there is only space, and thus one contemplates that space has no boundaries.
By forming such a conception, it is therefore called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

Furthermore, having transcended that object of focus, the sphere of infinite space, one further conceives of the perceiving consciousness as also being infinite; therefore, it is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

"Furthermore, having transcended that consciousness which acts as the perceiver, one should further contemplate that both the perceiver and the perceived are entirely non-existent; therefore, it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness."

Furthermore, having transcended that state of nothingness, one should further contemplate the absence of those coarse perceptions while not being without subtle perceptions; therefore, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are called the four formless absorptions.
Furthermore, what are called the four immeasurable practices? They are as follows:
The immeasurable of loving-kindness, the immeasurable of compassion, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy, and the immeasurable of equanimity.
If there is a bhikṣu who possesses a mind of great loving-kindness, he regards all sentient beings without enmity or favoritism, being able to bestow happiness upon them equally.
Thus, constantly practicing the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) is therefore called the "immeasurable practice of loving-kindness.

If there is a bhikṣu who possesses the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), who, toward all sentient beings, is without enmity or partiality and is able to equally uproot their suffering, and thus constantly practices the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*), this is therefore called the "immeasurable practice of compassion."

"If there is a bhikṣu who possesses a mind of great joy, who, toward all sentient beings, is without enmity or partiality, bestowing joy equally upon them, and thus constantly practices this immeasurable state of joy—therefore, it is called the practice of immeasurable joy."

"If there is a bhikṣu who, toward all sentient beings, dwells in equanimity without enmity or partiality, constantly practicing in this manner, it is therefore called the immeasurable practice of equanimity."
These are called the four immeasurable practices.
Furthermore, what are called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge? They are as follows:

The unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), and the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of expression: taking sound as its object, one possesses unimpeded mastery over all vocal sounds and verbal expressions.
Therefore, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of dharma (dharmapratisaṃvid). Regarding the unimpeded eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid):

this refers to the four types of analytical eloquence and the seven types of eloquence; in all instances of debate or inquiry, one is swift and unhindered. For this reason, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*):
it takes names, phrases, and syllables as its objects; whatever the teaching may be, there is nothing it does not penetrate.
Therefore, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena.
Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): taking meaning as its object, it understands every explained meaning without exception.
Therefore, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning.
These are what are known as the four unimpeded knowledges.
Furthermore, what are called the four perceptions of samādhi?
If a bhikṣu contemplates in this way:
"This body of mine, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, is composed of a collection of various impure things, such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, and bones."
For example, it is like a granary where grain and measures of rice are stored in great abundance; when a person enters within, they can skillfully distinguish, "This is rice;
this is wheat. Such a collection is called a granary.
When a bhikṣu contemplates his own body in this manner, he likewise attains the dharma that severs craving; this is called the first contemplation of samādhi.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has contemplated the body, he attains the flavor of pliancy within samādhi.
He then reflects further:

"This flavor of bliss obtained through samādhi is likewise devoid of conceptualization (saṃjñā). It is like a lotus flower that grows from water; the flower itself has no thought that 'I have emerged from the water and am cool.'"
It is the same for a bhikṣu’s contemplative visualization!
One who is able to visualize thus attains the taste of the bliss of mental pliancy (praśrabdhi) through seeing the Dharma; this is called the second samādhi-visualization.
"Furthermore, monks!
Regarding meditative concentration (samādhi), one should form the perception of light:
observe it as being like the sun, free from all darkness."
Observing in this manner with uninterrupted continuity, whether in light or darkness by day or night, there is no difference; one forms this perception of clarity, pure and unmixed.

It is like the autumn time when clouds and mists shroud the sun so that its light does not appear; yet if a person with clear vision contemplates the sunlight, they perceive it as pure and free from admixture.
So too is it for a bhikṣu when he practices contemplation!
One who is able to perform this visualization will immediately attain the manifestation of clear wisdom; this is called the third samādhi-visualization.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu is in samādhi, he performs this visualization:
he eliminates both suffering and pleasure, as well as sorrow and joy, until there remains only the two kinds of purity—equanimity and mindfulness.
For example, just as a person who can drive a chariot travels upon level ground without obstruction, so too it is with a bhikṣu’s contemplative visualization!
One who is able to visualize thus attains the manifestation of the excellence of wisdom; this is called the fourth samādhi-contemplation.
These are called the four perceptions of samādhi.
Furthermore, what are the dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness? They are as follows:
The body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the body as impure,
filled with foulness and devoid of reality— contemplating in this manner is called the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
"Furthermore, one contemplates that all sensations, whether internal or external, are entirely suffering; to practice such contemplation is called the foundation of mindfulness of sensation."

"Furthermore, one contemplates that both the mind and mental factors are entirely impermanent; one who practices such contemplation is said to dwell in mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the two categories of internal and external phenomena, and within these phenomena, does not give rise to the notion of a self; one who practices such contemplation is said to dwell in mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)."
These are called the dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, what are called the dharmas of the four right endeavors? They are as follows:

"Regarding unwholesome states that have already arisen, one should arouse diligence and apply oneself with effort to eliminate them, bringing them entirely to cessation; this is called the first right abandonment (samyakprahāṇa).

Furthermore, regarding unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, one should arouse diligence to guard against and eliminate them, ensuring they do not arise at all; this is called the second right abandonment."

"Furthermore, regarding wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one should arouse diligence so that all wholesome states may come into being and grow; this is called the third method of right abandonment."

Furthermore, regarding wholesome states that have already arisen, one should arouse diligence so that they may increase, become firm, and reach fulfillment; this is called the fourth method of right abandonment.
These are called the four dharmas of right exertion.
Furthermore, what are the four dharmas of the bases of psychic power? They are as follows:
Desire, diligence, mind, and investigation. If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding all defiled phenomena,

abandons deluded thoughts, and regarding all wholesome phenomena, gives rise to aspiration, progressing toward the good without weariness— this is called the base of psychic power of desire (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*).
"Furthermore, diligently cultivating all practices regarding wholesome dharmas and not retreating from right conduct is called the basis of psychic power of diligence.
Furthermore, abandoning erroneous reflection regarding all dharmas and correctly discerning with the mind is called the basis of psychic power of the mind."

Furthermore, with right wisdom, one observes the internal body; within the internal body there is no self. One further observes external objects; in external objects there are no phenomena. Since the essence of both self and phenomena is non-existent, one proceeds to realize the two kinds of emptiness.
This is called the supernormal power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-ṛddhipāda*). These are what are known as the four bases of supernormal power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
Furthermore, what are the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*)?
That is to say:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
These are called the five faculties.
Furthermore, what are called the five powers? They are:
the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
These are called the five powers.
Furthermore, what are the factors of the seven limbs of enlightenment? They are as follows:

The enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of concentration.
This is called the Dharma of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
Furthermore, what is called the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path? It is as follows:
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Regarding these,
"right view" means having faith that there is the law of giving, faith that there are parents, and faith that there are various wholesome and unwholesome actions.
Thus, for such wholesome and unwholesome karmas, there will indeed be retribution.

There are future worlds; within those worlds, there are sentient beings and there are Arhats who, practicing according to the truth, perceive such dharmas through their own supernormal powers: "My births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I shall not undergo further existence."
Such matters as these are called right view.
What is called right intention? It is as follows:
To be free from wrong intention (wherein wrong intention refers to the arising of improper views and the manifestation of greed, hatred, and delusion)—
to distance oneself from such as this is called right intention.
"What is called right speech?
It refers to being free from false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech; this is called right speech."
"What is called right action?
It refers to being free from such things as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; this is called right action."
"What is called right livelihood?
It means:

possessing right view, having gone forth into homelessness by means of the True Dharma, donning the dharma robes, remaining free from all wrong conduct, and having faith in the True Dharma; even down to the use of food, drink, sitting, and lying down, all are in accordance with the True Dharma—this is called right livelihood."
"What is called right diligence?
It means:
being free from wrong exertion."
To arouse right effort toward the true Dharma is called right effort.
What is called right mindfulness? It is as follows:
To be free from wrong thoughts,
constantly recollecting the True Dharma, keeping it in mind without forgetting or losing it— this is called right mindfulness.
What is called right concentration?
That is to say:

when the mind and mental factors do not give rise to distraction, are free from all objects of attachment, and engage in definitive and correct contemplation regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
"This is what is called the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One further addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that the definitive Right Dharma which I have proclaimed is good in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching; it is pure, unadulterated, and perfectly complete."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the assembly of bhikṣus was filled with great joy; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning Spoken by the Buddha.
